source_text: XXVI. Porro hujusmodi decreto subjacere contendunt non tantum bonas causarum liberarum actiones, verum etiam malas: Utrasque enim Deo decernente & volente fieri. Caeterum decretum illud absolutum & energeticum distinguunt in decretum effectivum quo Deus constituit aliquid efficere, & in decretum permissivum quo Deus constituit aliquid permittere. Isti autem Dei decreto effectivo subjiciunt non tantum bonas creaturarum actiones, verum etiam malas, si considerentur in se, & secundum illud quod in iis positivum est, ac prout distinguuntur a malitia quae ipsas denominat. Etenim has & illas fieri existimant Deo non solum decernente, sed etiam causas secundas ciente & movente, & ad hoc aut illud agendum applicante & determinante. Ipsam autem actionum liberarum malitiam a Deo non effici, sed permitti tantum docent.
english: They further contend that not only the good actions of free causes but also the evil ones fall under a decree of this kind, since both are done by God's decree and will. They divide that absolute and energetic decree into an effective decree, by which God resolved to bring something about, and a permissive decree, by which God resolved to permit something.

Under God's effective decree they place not only the good actions of creatures but also the evil ones, considered in themselves, according to what is positive in them, and as distinguished from the malice that gives them their name. They think both kinds are done not only by God's decree but also by his stirring and moving the second causes, applying and determining them to do this or that.
The malice of free actions itself, however, they teach is not brought about by God but only permitted.

source_text: XXVII. Attamen decretum illud quo malum, qua tale, Deus permittere statuit, licet non effectivum, efficax tamen esse volunt: unde est quod omnia quae fiunt, tam bona quam mala, tribuunt decreto Dei, ut graeca voce vocant, energetico, quod postea subdividunt in effectivum & efficax. Nam juxta ipsos, non minus necesse est ut posito Dei decreto permissivo, malum Deo permittente fiat; quam posito Dei decreto effectivo, necesse est ut fiat bonum Deo probante & efficiente. Adeoque pertendunt vere dici posse & debere non solum quod Deus malum permittere velit, sed etiam quod velit malum fieri ipso permittente: Quia, scilicet, divina voluntas non tantum fertur in mali permissionem, sed etiam in eventum ipsius actionis malae.
english: Yet they hold that the decree by which God resolved to permit evil as such, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious. That is why they ascribe everything that is done, good and evil alike, to God's decree which they call, with a Greek word, 'energetic', and which they then subdivide into effective and efficacious.

On their view, once God's permissive decree is in place, it is no less necessary that evil be done with God permitting it than, once his effective decree is in place, that good be done with God approving and bringing it about.

So they insist that it can and should truly be said not only that God wills to permit evil, but also that he wills evil to be done by his permission. The reason is that the divine will is directed not only to permitting evil but also to the actual outcome of the evil action.

source_text: XXVIII. Nec tamen inde sequi putant Deum esse peccati autorem: quoniam licet malum Deo decernente fiat, nihilominus non fit Deo efficiente, sed creatura ex certa permissione Dei deficiente. Ac quamvis quod in actione mala positivum est ad Deum ut ad causam efficientem referatur, non tamen propterea Deus mali causa est, quia nempe actionis quantumvis malae entitas est bona, malitia vero formaliter in quadam rectitudinis privatione consistit.
english: They deny, however, that this makes God the author of sin. Evil happens as God has decreed, yet God is not the one who works it: it comes from the creature falling short, under a definite permission of God.

And although what is positive in an evil action is traced to God as its efficient cause, God is not for that reason the cause of evil. The being of an action, however evil, is good, whereas malice formally consists in a certain lack of rectitude.

source_text: XXIX. Quod si quis objiciat Deum plane videri autorem eorum quae vult esse & fieri, quoniam voluntas Dei est causa rerum, respondent quod aliud est velle rem aliquam per se, aliud velle rem quoad eventum. Deinde quod Deus primo & proprie vult non impedire peccatum: & tantum ex consequenti vult eventum peccati: quia quod Deus non impedit, ideo evenit quia non impedit.
english: If someone objects that God plainly appears to be the author of what he wills to be and to be done, since God's will is the cause of things, they reply that willing a thing for its own sake is one thing and willing a thing as to its outcome is another.
They add that God first and properly wills not to hinder sin, and wills the outcome of sin only as a consequence. For what God does not hinder comes about precisely because he does not hinder it.

source_text: XXX. Ac praeterea distinguunt duplicem Dei voluntatem, unam generalem, alteram specialem. Specialis voluntas ipsis est qua Deus aliquid simul approbat & efficit. Atque voluntatis hujus objectum ab ea pendet, & eam sequitur ut effectus causam. Qua voluntate docent Deum velle bonum, & malum qua malum nolle, juxta illud, Deus non volens iniquitatem es tu. Voluntas vero generalis ex eorum sententia est, qua Deus vult aliquid non esse, vultque etiam certis de causis quaedam non prohibere & consequenter vult evenire, quae tamen simpliciter non probat: sive est decretum Dei, quo vult aliquid non quoad approbationem, & quoad effectionem a se, sed tantum quoad permissam quandam effectionem ab aliis: & sic, inquiunt, res facienda non pendet a voluntate Dei, sed tantum a voluntate deficientis creaturae. Atque hac voluntate dicunt Deum velle peccatum, ut lapsum Adami exempli gratia, non quidem simpliciter, sed solum quia vult illud evenire.
english: They also distinguish two wills in God, one general and the other special. The special will, for them, is that by which God both approves and brings about something. Its object depends on it and follows from it as an effect follows its cause. By this will, on their account, God wills what is good and is unwilling toward evil as evil, as in the verse, 'You are a God who does not will iniquity.'

The general will, on their view, is that by which God wills something not to be, and also, for definite reasons, wills not to forbid certain things and so wills them to come about, though he does not simply approve them. Or it is God's decree by which he wills something not as approving it or doing it himself, but only as a permitted doing by others.

And so, they say, the thing to be done depends not on God's will but only on the will of the failing creature. By this will, they say, God wills sin, the fall of Adam for example, not simply but only in that he wills it to come about.

source_text: XXXI. Ut vero necessitatem illam, quam Dei decretum quibuslibet eventibus imponit, cum eorum contingentia & libertate concilient, distinguunt primo inter necessitatem absolutam & necessitatem quae est ex hypothesi. Necessitas absoluta est qua simpliciter aliquid aliter esse non potest. Necessitas autem ex hypothesi est, qua quod in se & simpliciter potest non esse, vel aliter esse, posita tamen certa conditione, aliter se habere non potest. Deinde necessitas ab ipsis distinguitur in eam quae est coactionis, & eam quae est tantum infallibilitatis. Necessitas coactionis est, quae per causam extra agentem vim rebus infert, & coacte impellit ut hoc vel illud faciant. Necessitas vero infallibilitatis est, qua res quoad eventum certo & immutabiliter futura est: ita tamen ut si causam rei per se spectemus, possit vel non evenire, vel aliter evenire. Qua de necessitate intelligendum est illud axioma, Omne quod est, dum est, necessario est.
english: To reconcile the necessity that God's decree places on every event with the contingency and freedom of those events, they first distinguish absolute necessity from necessity on a hypothesis. Absolute necessity is that by which something simply cannot be otherwise. Necessity on a hypothesis is that by which something that in itself and simply can fail to be, or be otherwise, cannot be otherwise once a certain condition is given.

Next they divide necessity into the necessity of coercion and the necessity of mere infallibility. The necessity of coercion is that by which a cause acting from outside applies force to things and drives them by compulsion to do this or that.

The necessity of infallibility is that by which a thing is certainly and unchangeably going to happen, yet such that, if we look at the thing's cause in itself, it could fail to happen or happen otherwise. This is the necessity meant in the axiom, 'Everything that is, while it is, is necessarily.'

source_text: XXXII. His positis distinctionibus, dicunt ea quae fiunt a causis liberis & contingentibus necessario quidem evenire, respectu decreti divini, verum non absolute sed solum ex decreti illius hypothesi; nec eam necessitatem esse coactionis sed tantum infallibilitatis, quia nimirum Deus praeordinavit ut fierent: istud vero necessitatis genus causarum secundarum libertatem non tollere, sed potius stabilire: quoniam videlicet libertas & necessitas non se invicem perimunt, sed libertas & coactio. Nam, inquiunt, ex decreto Dei non tantum necesse est ut causa contingens & libera agat, sed etiam ut agat contingenter & libere: quia Deus decreto suo non solum determinavit singulos rerum eventus, sed etiam eorum modum & rationem.
english: With these distinctions in place, they say that what free and contingent causes do does indeed come about necessarily with respect to the divine decree. But it does so not absolutely, only on the hypothesis of that decree; and the necessity is not one of coercion but only of infallibility, because God foreordained that these things should be done.
This kind of necessity, they say, does not remove the freedom of second causes but rather secures it, since it is not freedom and necessity that cancel each other out but freedom and coercion.

'For,' they say, 'God's decree makes it necessary not only that a contingent and free cause act, but also that it act contingently and freely. By his decree God determined not only each event but also its mode and manner.'

source_text: XXXIII. Quibus addunt, Deum movere causas liberas prout illarum naturae congruum & consentaneum est, nempe voluntatem molliter flectendo, & per objecta ab intellectu monstrata inclinando, nec aliter quam ut homo de eo quod acturus est secum consultet atque deliberet, & ex proprio judicio quod sibi sequendum videatur eligat. Quinimo causam liberam sic a Dei decreto, & quae decretum sequitur motione determinari ad hoc sive istud agendum, ut tamen simul in ea maneat potestas non agendi & aliter agendi, non quidem in sensu composito sed in sensu diviso: quia licet cum divina praeordinatione ad hunc aut illum actum non consistat actus oppositus aut cessatio ab eodem actu, optime tamen cum ea consistit potestas ad actum contrarium, aut ad ipsius actus suspensionem: Quae doctrina est Gulielmi Perkinsi in libello de praedestinationis modo & ordine, & Tuissi illius vindicis, & complurium aliorum clarissimorum apud Reformatos virorum, ut prolixe videre est apud eundem Tuissum toto libro secundo vindiciarum libelli istius Perkinsiani.
english: They add that God moves free causes in a way suited and agreeable to their nature: by gently bending the will and inclining it through objects shown to it by the intellect, and only in such a way that a man consults and deliberates with himself about what he will do, and chooses by his own judgement what seems to him the course to follow.

They say further that a free cause is so determined to do this or that by God's decree, and by the motion that follows the decree, that there still remains in it the power not to act and to act otherwise, not in the composite sense but in the divided sense.

For although the opposite act, or ceasing from that act, cannot stand together with God's preordination to this or that act, the power to the contrary act, or to suspending the act, stands with it perfectly well.

This is the teaching of William Perkins in his little book on the mode and order of predestination, of Twisse who defended him, and of many other very distinguished men among the Reformed. It can be seen at length in Twisse, throughout the second book of his defence of Perkins's little book.

source_text: XXXIV. Porro quanquam omnium Doctorum istorum virorum suspiciam ingenium & eruditionem, in nulla tamen ex dictis sententiis acquiescere possum. Non enim omnem scrupulum eximunt. Nec eorum ulla est quae non insigni quadam difficultate laborare mihi videatur.
english: For all my respect for the talent and learning of all these doctors, I cannot rest in any of the opinions described. They do not remove every doubt, and every one of them seems to me to struggle with some serious difficulty.

source_text: XXXV. Etenim sententia illa quae divinis decretis praestruit scientiam conditionatam de futura inclinatione & propensione voluntatis in hanc vel illam partem, si talis occasio agendi ipsi offeratur; Et quae statuit Deum non aliter praeordinavisse hominum actiones, quam quia voluit illos in eo statu creare, illasque occasiones agendi iis offerre, unde consequi praevidebat illos, mediante ipsius generali concursu, tali modo acturos, & has potius quam illas volitiones elicituros esse non necessitate quadam, vel ab objectis ipsis, vel ab aliqua Dei actione imposita, sed quia ipsi per se sic se essent determinaturi, cum contrarium esset in eorum potestate: haec, inquam, sententia multa quidem incommoda vitat quibus urgentur aliae sententiae: sed cum ea difficulter conciliari potest gratia victrix & per se efficax, quae liberum sibi subjicit arbitrium, minime vero libero arbitrio subjicienda est, quam praedicat Schola orthodoxa.
english: Take first the opinion that sets before the divine decrees a conditional knowledge of how the will would lean and incline, one way or the other, if a given occasion for acting were offered it. It holds that God foreordained men's actions only in that he willed to create them in that state and offer them those occasions for acting.

From this he foresaw that, with his general concurrence, they would act in such a way and would produce these volitions rather than those. They would do so not by any necessity laid on them by the objects themselves or by some action of God, but because they would so determine themselves of their own accord, the contrary being in their power.

This opinion, I say, does avoid many of the awkward consequences that press on the others. But it can hardly be reconciled with the grace that conquers and is efficacious of itself, which brings free choice under itself and is by no means to be made subject to free choice, as the orthodox School proclaims.

source_text: XXXVI. Adde quod, etsi Deus, priusquam aliquid de nobis decernat, praesciat quid voluntas factura sit, ex hypothesi quod constituatur in talibus circumstantiis, & ejusmodi motiva accedant; tamen si Deus aliquid simpliciter futurum praefinit, ante praevisam absolute voluntatis nostrae determinationem, inde nascitur quaedam necessitas antecedens, quandoquidem quod Deus praedefinit omnino necesse est fore: quae necessitas non minus libertati repugnare videtur, quam si nulla talis scientia conditionata praecessisset, cum scientia ista non faciat ut tale Dei decretum sit in nostra potestate.
english: Add this. Suppose that before decreeing anything about us God foreknows what the will would do on the supposition that it is placed in such circumstances and such motives are brought to bear. Still, if God foreordains something as simply going to happen before the absolute determination of our will is foreseen, an antecedent necessity arises from it, since what God predefines must without fail come to be.
This necessity seems no less at odds with freedom than if no such conditional knowledge had gone before, since that knowledge does not put such a decree of God in our power.

source_text: XXXVII. In sententia Joan. Strangii illud omnino mihi videtur improbabile, quod inter eas quae ab hominibus consulto & deliberate fiunt, discrimen quoad libertatem statuit; quasi quaedam duntaxat liberae essent ea libertate quae sita est in indifferentia, & per quam homo potest agere vel non agere; hoc vel illud agere, aliae vero solum libertate simplici ad quam non requiritur voluntatis indeterminatio, sed tantum ut homo sponte & cum judicio agat. Ad quod genus pertinere putat, non solum omnes actiones bonas, sed etiam multas quae ex suo genere nec bonae, nec malae sunt. Cum enim experiamur nos eodem modo uti ratione & judicio nostro, ac eligendi potestate, non tantum in omnibus vitae civilis actionibus, sed etiam in bonis, quare putabimus alias aliis magis esse liberas, neque eandem libertatis speciem omnibus competere?
english: In John Strang's opinion, what seems to me quite improbable is the difference he sets up, as regards freedom, among things men do on purpose and after deliberation. As he has it, only some acts are free with the freedom that lies in indifference, by which a man can act or not act, do this or that, while others are free only with a simple freedom that does not require the will's indetermination, only that a man act willingly and with judgement.

To this second class, he thinks, belong not only all good actions but also many that in their kind are neither good nor evil. Yet we find by experience that we use our reason, judgement and power of choice in the same way, not only in all the actions of civil life but also in good ones. Why, then, should we think that some acts are freer than others, and that the same kind of freedom does not belong to them all?

source_text: XXXVIII. Praeterea vero quid cogit ut dicamus Deum, dum nos movet ad bona opera, a nobis auferre per gratiam suam potestatem aliter agendi, cum sine hoc constare possit gratiae divinae sua efficacia: nec desint sapientiae divinae rationes quibus praestet ut hoc agamus, idque certo ac infallibiliter, quanquam a nobis non tollat potentiam ad actum oppositum, & ad nostri etiam actus suspensionem?
english: Besides, what forces us to say that when God moves us to good works he takes from us, by his grace, the power to act otherwise? Divine grace can have its efficacy without this.
Nor does divine wisdom lack ways to ensure that we do the good, and do it certainly and infallibly, even though it does not take from us the power to the opposite act, or even to suspend our act.

source_text: XXXIX. Istud quoque non placet in sententia Mosis Amyraldi, quod supponit mentem atque voluntatem in omnibus suis actibus ab objectis sic determinari, ut si haec vel illa eis objiciantur, tali modo ac ratione, necessario hoc aut illud agant, neque possint aliter agere, aut ab actione cessare. Si enim potentiae rationales non minus quam brutae ad certam actionem determinentur a suis objectis, quodnam erit discrimen inter brutorum spontaneos motus, & liberas actiones creaturarum rationalium? Et quomodo dici poterunt agentia libera actuum suorum domini, & in sua potestate proprios actus habere, si objecta ipsis, non minus quam agentibus caeteris, necessitatem agendi imponant?
english: In Moses Amyraut's opinion, too, I am not satisfied with his assumption that in all their acts the mind and will are so determined by objects that, if these or those are set before them in a certain way and manner, they necessarily do this or that and cannot act otherwise or stop acting.

If rational powers, no less than brute ones, are determined to a given action by their objects, what difference will there be between the spontaneous motions of animals and the free actions of rational creatures?
And how can free agents be called masters of their acts and be said to have their own acts in their power, if objects impose a necessity of acting on them no less than on other agents?

source_text: XL. Praesertim si concipiamus primo homini fuisse necessitatem impositam edendi de fructu vetito, per objecta quae, juxta Dei decretum, & divina providentia procurante & administrante, ipsi oblata fuerunt; nec Adamum potuisse ab eo abstinere, habita ratione, tum virium quas a Deo acceperat, tum incitamentorum quibus ad hoc fuit inductus, non video quae in eo fuerit culpa supplicio digna, & quomodo Deus non sit peccati ejus autor, cum esus iste illicitus necessario secutus sit ex proportione virium quas Deus ipsi indulserat, cum tentationibus & objectis variis, quae, nulla ejus culpa, sed Deo sic ordinante ac disponente, ipsi proposita sunt.
english: This is especially so if we suppose that a necessity of eating the forbidden fruit was laid on the first man through objects offered to him according to God's decree, with divine providence arranging and managing it. Suppose too that Adam could not refrain from it, given both the strength he had received from God and the incitements by which he was led to it.

Then I do not see what fault there was in him that deserved punishment, or how God is not the author of his sin. That unlawful eating would have followed necessarily from the match between the strength God had granted him and the temptations and various objects set before him, not by any fault of his but because God so ordained and arranged it.

source_text: XLI. Denique in postrema, plurium tamen Doctorum illustrium, sententia probare non possumus, quod dicunt Deum velle ut mala fiant, licet ipso non efficiente, sed tantum permittente. Nec enim putamus Deum recte dici posse velle id quod non probat. At dici non potest mala fieri Deo approbante. Nec percipimus sensum distinctionis illius, qua distinguunt inter malum & inter mali eventum, & aiunt Deum malum quidem non velle, sed nihilominus velle mali eventum; Deumque mala ipsa nolle, sed tamen velle ut mala contingant; seu quod idem est, velle malorum existentiam quomodo potest enim existentia rei a re ipsa distingui, & qua ratione potest aliquis rem quampiam nolle, & simul velle ut res illa existat?
english: Finally, in the last opinion, though it is held by many illustrious doctors, we cannot accept their saying that God wills evils to be done, even though he does not bring them about but only permits them. We do not think God can rightly be said to will what he does not approve, and it cannot be said that evils are done with God's approval.

Nor can we see the sense of the distinction they draw between evil and the outcome of evil, when they say that God does not will evil yet does will the outcome of evil; that God refuses evils themselves yet wills that evils should happen; or, what amounts to the same, that he wills the existence of evils.
How can the existence of a thing be distinguished from the thing itself? And how can anyone refuse something and at the same time will that it exist?

source_text: XLII. Nec minus durum est quod dicunt decreto Dei effectivo praedefinitas esse illas ipsas actiones quibus necessario malitia annexa est. Quomodo enim Deus autor peccati non erit, si aeterno suo decreto praedefinivit actum illum quo aliquis Deum ipsum odit, & nomen illius blasphemat, & juxta decretum suum, hominem in tempore ad istam actus speciem praemovet & praedeterminat?
english: No less harsh is their claim that the very actions to which malice is necessarily attached were predefined by God's effective decree.

How will God not be the author of sin if by his eternal decree he predefined the act by which someone hates God himself and blasphemes his name, and in time, in line with his decree, premoves and predetermines the man to that kind of act?

source_text: XLIII. Idem absurdum videtur ex eo manifeste sequi quod dicunt malum etiam qua malum, praeordinatum esse decreto Dei, quod licet effectivum non sit, nihilominus efficax est, & tale ut, eo posito, necessario malum consequatur. Quid enim, an dicemus ex Dei decreto necesse fuisse ut primus homo in Deum rebellaret, & mandatum ab eo acceptum transgrederetur? Ac quomodo potuit juste ob peccatum puniri, cui citra ullam antecedentem culpam, imposita fuit peccandi necessitas? Et annon potius istius transgressionis culpa debet in eum refundi, a cujus decreto necessitas tam dura orta fuisse supponitur?
english: The same absurdity seems plainly to follow from their saying that evil, even as evil, was foreordained by a decree of God which, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious, such that once it is in place evil necessarily follows.

What then? Shall we say that God's decree made it necessary for the first man to rebel against God and break the command he had received from him? How could he justly be punished for sin if a necessity of sinning was laid on him without any prior fault?
And should not the guilt of that transgression rather be thrown back on him from whose decree so harsh a necessity is supposed to have arisen?

source_text: XLIV. Scio magnos illos viros qui locutionibus ejusmodi utuntur, consequentias istas non admittere, & dicta sua quantum possunt reducere ad sensum bonum atque commodum: sed quantumvis ejusmodi durae locutiones interpretatione benigna emolliantur, Christianae plebis aures non possunt non offendere, & animis audientium non injicere varios scrupulos, absque ulla necessitate. Quid enim opus mordicus adhaerere istis loquendi modis, qui nec diserte sunt in scriptura expressi, nec sunt in usu veterum Ecclesiae Doctorum?
english: I know that the great men who use expressions of this kind do not admit these consequences, and bring their statements, as far as they can, to a sound and acceptable sense.

But however much such harsh expressions are softened by charitable interpretation, they cannot fail to offend the ears of Christian people and to plant various doubts in the minds of those who hear them, and that without any need. What need is there to cling tooth and nail to ways of speaking that are neither stated outright in Scripture nor used by the ancient doctors of the Church?

source_text: XLV. At inquiet aliquis quid alienas sententias carpis? Si melius quid habes accerse, vel imperium fer. Respondeo, quaedam in hoc negotio apud me certa esse atque indubitata, alia vero a me ignorari. Ex scriptura clarum est, & ratio quoque ipsa astipulatur omnia Dei providentia regi, & ita subesse decretis divinis, ut nihil Deo inscio sive invito fiat. Quicquid bene fit, ad illum ut bonorum omnium authorem referendum esse; sed malorum omnium culpam penes creaturam solam residere. Nihil tamen mali contingere, nisi quantum Deus certo consilio sinit & non impedit; Deumque sic moderari malas hominum actiones, illisque ea ratione uti, ut inde multa bona eliciat, illasque ad varios & optimos fines dirigat.
english: Someone will say: 'Why do you pick at other men's opinions? If you have something better, bring it out, or else take orders.' I answer that in this matter some things are certain and beyond doubt for me, while others I do not know.

It is clear from Scripture, and reason itself agrees, that all things are governed by God's providence and are so subject to the divine decrees that nothing happens without God's knowledge or against his will. Whatever is done well is to be credited to him as the author of all good things, while the guilt of all evils lies with the creature alone.

Yet nothing evil happens except so far as God, by a settled plan, allows it and does not hinder it. And God so governs men's evil actions, and uses them in such a way, that he draws many good things from them and directs them to various excellent ends.

source_text: XLVI. Nec minus ratione & experientia certum, & etiam scripturae authoritate confirmatum, homines seu bene, sive male agant, libertate sua uti, & ita libere moveri, ut laude vel vituperio, vel poena vel praemio merito digni habeantur, prout bene vel male egerint.
english: It is no less certain by reason and experience, and confirmed also by the authority of Scripture, that men use their freedom whether they act well or badly. They are moved so freely that they are rightly held to deserve praise or blame, punishment or reward, according as they have acted well or badly.

source_text: XLVII. Ex quibus consequitur sic agnoscendam esse libertatem humanam, ut tamen providentiae divinae nihil derogetur; & contra, vim & efficaciam providentiae Divinae sic extollendam esse, ut tamen creaturae libertas sua asseratur. Caeterum, modo salva sit creaturae rationalis in agendo libertas, & diligenter caveatur, ne creaturae culpa in Deum transferatur, quasi peccati causa vel author esset, providentiae divinae decretis & efficaciae nimium non posse tribui.
english: It follows that human freedom must be acknowledged in a way that takes nothing away from divine providence, and that the power and efficacy of divine providence must be exalted in a way that still affirms the creature's freedom.

But provided the rational creature's freedom in acting is kept intact, and great care is taken not to shift the creature's guilt onto God, as if he were the cause or author of sin, one cannot ascribe too much to the decrees and efficacy of divine providence.

source_text: XLVIII. Sed sigillatim exponere quae sit decretorum divinorum ratio, & qua ratione Deus creaturas rationales sic regat & moveat, ut naturae suae congruenter, id est, libere semper agant, fateor rem esse quae captum meum superat. Non dubito quin sapientiae & potentiae divinae, quae utraque infinita est, rationes abunde suppetant quibus id praestent effectum; sed illas assequi, non puto tenuitatis esse meae. Nec enim in iis quae legi aut excogitare potui quicquam inveni quod mihi omni ex parte satisfaceret, & in quo animus, tanquam re comperta & percepta, posset acquiescere. Itaque malo ingenue ignorantiam meam hac in parte fateri, quam jactare me scire, quae ipse nescire mihi conscius sum: & aliis tanquam vera obtrudere, de quorum veritate non sum ipse plene persuasus.
english: But to explain point by point the nature of the divine decrees, and how God so governs and moves rational creatures that they always act in keeping with their nature, that is, freely, is, I confess, beyond my understanding.

I do not doubt that divine wisdom and power, both of them infinite, have ample means of achieving this. But I do not think it lies within my small capacity to grasp them. In all I have been able to read or think out, I have found nothing that satisfied me on every side, nothing in which the mind could rest as in something found out and understood.
So I would rather frankly confess my ignorance on this point than boast that I know what I am aware I do not know, or press on others as true things whose truth I am not fully convinced of myself.

source_text: XLIX. Nec me pudet hujus meae ignorantiae. Tuto enim ignoratur, quod nec Deus aperte in verbo suo revelavit, nec humana ratio per se investigare potest. Jam autem scriptura sacra manifeste docet quidem, omnia divina providentia regi, nec quicquam, nisi ipso consulto sinente, fieri, & ab aeterno Deo nota esse & definita omnia opera sua: modum vero quo Deus causas secundas movet, quae sit ratio decretorum illius, & qua ratione illa exequatur, & omnia ad finem destinatum perducat, scriptura sacra non aperit, nec studet humanae curiositati super eo satisfacere.
english: I am not ashamed of this ignorance of mine. It is safe not to know what God has not openly revealed in his word and what human reason cannot search out by itself.

Holy Scripture does plainly teach that all things are governed by divine providence, that nothing happens unless he deliberately allows it, and that all his works are known to God and settled from eternity.

But how God moves second causes, what the nature of his decrees is, how he carries them out and brings all things to their appointed end, Holy Scripture does not disclose, nor does it seek to satisfy human curiosity on the point.

source_text: L. Imo satis indicat rem esse quam Deus voluit humanis ingeniis esse occultam atque imperviam, & in cujus profundum mentis nostrae acies penetrare non valet. Quo pertinet illud Dei apud Isaiam. Non enim cogitationes meae, cogitationes vestrae; neque viae vestrae viae meae. Quia sicut exaltantur coeli a terra, sic exaltatae sunt viae meae a viis vestris, & cogitationes meae a cogitationibus vestris: Item illud Apostoli in epistola ad Romanos, O Altitudo divitiarum sapientiae & scientiae Dei: quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, & investigabiles viae ejus! Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini? Aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit?
english: Indeed, it shows clearly enough that this is something God willed to be hidden from human minds and closed to them, a depth our mind's sharpest sight cannot reach.

This is what God says in Isaiah: 'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so are my ways high above your ways and my thoughts above your thoughts.'

So too the Apostle in the letter to the Romans: 'O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgements, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?'

source_text: LI. Nec tamen propterea damno virorum Doctorum conatum, qui nituntur lucem aliquam his tenebris inferre, ac per se experiri quo possit in re tanta animus noster assurgere; modo id fiat cum debita modestia, & vera ac seria imbecillitatis nostrae agnitione: & ita sic quisque proprii ingenii conjecturas & commenta proferat, ut aliorum etiam rationes audiat, nec putet se solum sapere, acerbe & hostiliter contendens & rixans cum iis, qui se statim dictatis illius subjicere nolunt. Verum ista qualiacunque Scholae reservanda sunt, nec facile apud plebem movendae difficultates, quae eos scrupulos animis injiciunt, quos additae solutiones obscurae & infirmae discutere non valent.
english: Not that I therefore condemn the efforts of learned men who try to bring some light into this darkness and to test for themselves how high our mind can rise in so great a matter, provided it is done with proper modesty and a true and serious recognition of our weakness.

Let each put forward the conjectures and inventions of his own mind in such a way that he also listens to the reasoning of others. Let him not think he alone is wise, nor fight and quarrel bitterly and with hostility against those who will not at once submit to his pronouncements.

But such things, whatever they are worth, should be kept for the School. Difficulties should not lightly be raised among the people, for they plant doubts in men's minds that the obscure and weak solutions offered with them cannot clear away.
